items.stem: Define the term “speculation, elaboration and stabilisation”, and give one example.
items.answer: Hargreaves’s three stages through which teachers’ impressions of pupils become fixed labels. Example: a first impression hardening into a fixed view.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition (Hargreaves’s three stages through which teachers’ impressions of pupils become fixed labels); 1 mark for a relevant example such as a first impression hardening into a fixed view. [2]

items.stem: Explain the difference between “typing” and “speculation, elaboration and stabilisation”, using an example of each.
items.answer: Typing: the process by which teachers categorise pupils (e.g. seeing a pupil as a “conformist” or “deviant”). Speculation, elaboration and stabilisation: Hargreaves’s three stages through which teachers’ impressions of pupils become fixed labels (e.g. a first impression hardening into a fixed view).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each accurate definition; 1 mark each relevant example. [4]

items.stem: A new teacher in Seoul decides in the first lesson that Ines is “lazy”; by the end of term the teacher no longer asks Ines any questions. Suggest how a Marxist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Marxism: education reproduces class inequality and legitimates it: the hidden curriculum prepares working-class pupils for subordinate jobs (Bowles and Gintis), schools act as ideological state apparatuses (Althusser), and the myth of meritocracy makes failure seem the individual’s fault.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: A new teacher in Accra decides in the first lesson that Hana is “lazy”; by the end of term the teacher no longer asks Hana any questions. Explain how a New Right sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: New Right: state education is inefficient and does not meet the needs of the economy; competition, parental choice and a market in schools will raise standards (Chubb and Moe), while education should transmit a shared national culture.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the strengths and limitations of using structured interviews to research pupils’ views of their teachers.
items.answer: Strengths: the interviewer can read questions aloud, so younger or less literate respondents can take part; answers can be quantified and compared between social groups. Limitations: the interview is an artificial social encounter, so answers may not reflect real behaviour; they are more costly and time-consuming than questionnaires because interviewers must be trained and paid. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying pupils’ views of their teachers but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: A sociologist in Karachi wants to research the effects of setting on pupils’ self-esteem. Evaluate the use of unstructured interviews for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: a sympathetic, non-judgemental interviewer can help people talk about painful or private experiences; the interviewer can follow up answers and explore meanings in the interviewee’s own words. Limitations: the power imbalance between adult researcher and child may make children say what they think adults want to hear; samples are small, so findings are difficult to generalise. Theory: unstructured interviews are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the effects of setting on pupils’ self-esteem but best combined with another method such as longitudinal studies (following the same sample over time) (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: A research team is investigating anti-school subcultures in Muscat. Evaluate the use of covert participant observation for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: it may be the only way to study a group that hides its activities from outsiders; because the group does not know it is being studied, members act naturally and the Hawthorne effect is avoided. Limitations: studying children covertly is ethically unacceptable because they cannot consent and are vulnerable; the study cannot be repeated, so reliability is low. Theory: covert participant observation is favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produces qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying anti-school subcultures in Muscat but best combined with another method such as non-participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Diego, a sociology student, is designing a project on anti-school subcultures in Lisbon. Evaluate the use of self-completion questionnaires for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: they can reach a large, geographically spread sample quickly and cheaply, so findings can be generalised; they are standardised, so the study can be repeated by another researcher to check reliability. Limitations: younger respondents may misread questions or lack the concentration to complete them carefully, and may answer as they think adults expect; they measure what people say they do, not what they actually do. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying anti-school subcultures in Lisbon but best combined with another method such as semi-structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Mei found this account of a study (Source A) while revising. “A researcher spent a year in a school in Dhaka, attending lessons and spending break times with a group of Year 10 pupils. Pupils in the bottom set described school as “a joke” and gained respect from friends for answering back to teachers. Top-set pupils described their bottom-set peers as “wasting their chance”.” (a) Explain one limitation of the method used in Source A for studying pupil subcultures. (b) Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that setting is the main cause of anti-school subcultures.
items.answer: (a) It is time-consuming, costly and may put the researcher at risk. (b) For: The source shows anti-school attitudes concentrated in the bottom set; Lacey and Ball link differentiation to polarisation. Against: Willis shows class culture shapes subcultures before setting; Woods shows varied adaptations; the researcher’s presence may have changed behaviour; one school may be untypical. Also consider how far a single study using participant observation can support a general claim. Judgement: a reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for a relevant limitation; 1 mark for applying it to the study in the source. [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple points from the source or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): explained points for and against using the source and own knowledge. Level 3 (5-6): balanced, well-supported evaluation with comment on the evidence and a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Read Source A. “A researcher spent a year in a school in Toronto, attending lessons and spending break times with a group of Year 10 pupils. Pupils in the bottom set described school as “a joke” and gained respect from friends for answering back to teachers. Top-set pupils described their bottom-set peers as “wasting their chance”.” (a) Using Source A, identify two findings of the study. (b) Explain how an interactionist sociologist might interpret the findings in Source A. (c) Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that setting is the main cause of anti-school subcultures.
items.answer: (a) 1. Bottom-set pupils gained respect for answering back to teachers. 2. Top-set pupils described bottom-set peers as “wasting their chance”. (b) The findings show polarisation: pupils labelled and placed in low sets suffer status frustration and form an anti-school subculture, while top-set pupils become pro-school (Lacey). (c) For: The source shows anti-school attitudes concentrated in the bottom set; Lacey and Ball link differentiation to polarisation. Against: Willis shows class culture shapes subcultures before setting; Woods shows varied adaptations; the researcher’s presence may have changed behaviour; one school may be untypical. Also consider how far a single study using participant observation can support a general claim. Judgement: a reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for each finding taken from the source. [2] (b) 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the findings in the source. [3] (c) Level 1 (1-2): simple points from the source or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): explained points for and against using the source and own knowledge. Level 3 (5-6): balanced, well-supported evaluation with comment on the evidence and a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: A sociologist in Nairobi wants to research teacher-pupil interaction in mathematics lessons. Evaluate the use of self-completion questionnaires for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: they are standardised, so the study can be repeated by another researcher to check reliability; there is no interviewer present, so interviewer bias is avoided and anonymity is easier to guarantee. Limitations: younger respondents may misread questions or lack the concentration to complete them carefully, and may answer as they think adults expect; respondents may misunderstand questions, or give socially desirable answers, and there is no chance to clarify. Theory: self-completion questionnaires are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying teacher-pupil interaction in mathematics lessons but best combined with another method such as unstructured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: In a classroom in Muscat, pupils agree to complete a worksheet quietly if the teacher lets them choose where to sit. Explain how an interactionist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Interactionism: what happens inside schools matters: teachers’ labels, setting and streaming and pupils’ responses (subcultures) shape achievement through self-fulfilling prophecies (Becker, Rist, Keddie).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Mohammed is planning a study of pupils’ views of their teachers. Evaluate the use of personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) for this research.
items.answer: Strengths: they show how people themselves understood their experiences; they give an insight into people’s feelings and meanings in their own words, so validity can be high. Limitations: their meaning must be interpreted by the researcher, which may introduce bias; they may not be authentic or credible; the writer may exaggerate or present themselves favourably. Theory: personal documents (diaries, letters, blogs and social media posts) are favoured mainly by interpretivist sociologists and produce qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying pupils’ views of their teachers but best combined with another method such as structured interviews (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): one or two simple points about the method. Level 2 (3-4): explains strengths OR limitations applied to the context. Level 3 (5-6): explains strengths AND limitations applied to the context with a supported judgement. [6]

items.stem: Which term describes teaching pupils of different abilities together in the same class?
items.answer: Mixed-ability teaching
items.markingKey: Mixed-ability teaching: teaching pupils of different abilities together in the same class. [1]

items.stem: A student writes: “Setting and streaming mean the same thing.” Is this correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Setting groups pupils by ability in each subject; streaming groups them by general ability for all subjects.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the correct judgement; 1 mark for an accurate sociological explanation. [2]

items.stem: Lacey argued that streaming leads to differentiation and polarisation among pupils. Explain this view and one criticism of it.
items.answer: Lacey’s study of Hightown Grammar found boys in lower streams formed anti-school subcultures, while top-stream boys became more pro-school. Criticism: It was a single boys’ grammar school.
items.markingKey: Up to 2 marks for explaining the view (Interactionism); up to 2 marks for an explained criticism. [4]

items.stem: Study the data, which come from a study of setting and exam tier (200 pupils, Santiago). Table: percentage of pupils entered for the higher-tier exam | Middle-class pupils | Working-class pupils. Top set | 94% | 91%. Middle set | 56% | 53%. Bottom set | 25% | 22%. What is the difference, in percentage points, between Middle-class pupils and Working-class pupils for Bottom set (Working-class pupils minus Middle-class pupils)?
items.answer: -3 percentage points
items.markingKey: 22 − 25 = -3 percentage points. [1]

items.stem: In Seoul, a school abolishes setting and teaches all subjects in mixed-ability classes; teachers report that lower-attaining pupils participate more. Explain how a functionalist sociologist might interpret this situation.
items.answer: Functionalism: education performs vital functions for society: it passes on shared values and creates social solidarity (Durkheim), acts as a bridge from particularistic family values to universalistic values of wider society, and allocates people to roles on the basis of merit (Parsons, Davis and Moore).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying the key idea of the perspective; up to 2 marks for applying it to the details of the situation; 1 mark for a relevant concept or sociologist. [4]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of structured interviews for studying the effects of setting on pupils’ self-esteem.
items.answer: Strengths: the interviewer can read questions aloud, so younger or less literate respondents can take part; answers can be quantified and compared between social groups. Limitations: respondents may be reluctant to reveal sensitive information face to face to a stranger following a fixed script; they are more costly and time-consuming than questionnaires because interviewers must be trained and paid. Theory: structured interviews are favoured mainly by positivist sociologists and produce quantitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying the effects of setting on pupils’ self-esteem but best combined with another method such as covert participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-2): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (3-4): some explained strengths or limitations, weakly applied. Level 3 (5-6): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context, using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, ethics). Level 4 (7-8): well-developed, balanced evaluation applied to the context, with theoretical links (positivism/interpretivism) and a reasoned conclusion. [8]

items.stem: Which term describes a subculture whose members accept and value the school’s goals?
items.answer: Pro-school subculture
items.markingKey: Pro-school subculture: a subculture whose members accept and value the school’s goals. [1]

items.stem: Explain what sociologists mean by “conformity”.
items.answer: Woods’s adaptation in which pupils accept the school’s goals and means.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for a clear definition: Woods’s adaptation in which pupils accept the school’s goals and means. [1]

items.stem: Explain the difference between pro-school and anti-school subcultures, using an example of each.
items.answer: Pro-school pupils accept school values and gain status through success (e.g. top-set pupils joining clubs); anti-school pupils reject school values and gain status by breaking rules (e.g. Willis’s lads).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each definition; 1 mark each example. [4]

items.stem: Felix is planning a study of anti-school subcultures in Bogotá. Explain one limitation of using unstructured interviews for this research.
items.answer: The power imbalance between adult researcher and child may make children say what they think adults want to hear.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for identifying a relevant limitation; 1 mark for explaining it in the context of anti-school subcultures in Bogotá. [2]

items.stem: Chloe found this account of a study (Source A) while revising. “A researcher spent a year in a school in Hanoi, attending lessons and spending break times with a group of Year 10 pupils. Pupils in the bottom set described school as “a joke” and gained respect from friends for answering back to teachers. Top-set pupils described their bottom-set peers as “wasting their chance”.” (a) Identify the main research method used in the study described in Source A. (b) Using Source A, explain one strength of the method used for studying pupil subcultures.
items.answer: (a) Participant observation. (b) It records real behaviour, avoiding the gap between what people say and what they do.
items.markingKey: (a) Participant observation. [1] (b) 1 mark for a relevant strength; 1 mark for applying it to the study in the source. [2]

items.stem: In a school in Lima, a group of pupils organise a debating club and revise together for exams. Suggest how an interactionist sociologist might explain this.
items.answer: Interactionism: what happens inside schools matters: teachers’ labels, setting and streaming and pupils’ responses (subcultures) shape achievement through self-fulfilling prophecies (Becker, Rist, Keddie).
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the key idea of the perspective; 1 mark for applying it to the situation. [2]

items.stem: Read Source A. “A researcher spent a year in a school in Lima, attending lessons and spending break times with a group of Year 10 pupils. Pupils in the bottom set described school as “a joke” and gained respect from friends for answering back to teachers. Top-set pupils described their bottom-set peers as “wasting their chance”.” (a) Explain one limitation of the method used in Source A for studying pupil subcultures. (b) Using Source A and your own knowledge, evaluate the view that setting is the main cause of anti-school subcultures.
items.answer: (a) The researcher may become too involved and lose objectivity (“going native”). (b) For: The source shows anti-school attitudes concentrated in the bottom set; Lacey and Ball link differentiation to polarisation. Against: Willis shows class culture shapes subcultures before setting; Woods shows varied adaptations; the researcher’s presence may have changed behaviour; one school may be untypical. Also consider how far a single study using participant observation can support a general claim. Judgement: a reasoned conclusion.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark for a relevant limitation; 1 mark for applying it to the study in the source. [2] (b) Level 1 (1-2): simple points from the source or own knowledge. Level 2 (3-4): explained points for and against using the source and own knowledge. Level 3 (5-6): balanced, well-supported evaluation with comment on the evidence and a reasoned conclusion. [6]

items.stem: Evaluate the usefulness of non-participant observation for studying how pupils gain status among their peers.
items.answer: Strengths: children can be observed in classrooms or playgrounds without having to answer questions; it records behaviour as it happens rather than relying on people’s accounts. Limitations: the presence of an observer may change behaviour (the Hawthorne effect); observation schedules impose the researcher’s categories on behaviour. Theory: non-participant observation is favoured by both positivist and interpretivist (depending on how structured it is) sociologists and produces quantitative or qualitative data. Judgement: useful for some aims in studying how pupils gain status among their peers but best combined with another method such as participant observation (triangulation).
items.markingKey: Level 1 (1-3): simple, list-like points. Level 2 (4-6): explained strengths or limitations with some application. Level 3 (7-8): explained strengths and limitations applied to the context using concepts (validity, reliability, representativeness, practical and ethical issues). Level 4 (9-10): balanced, well-applied evaluation with theoretical links, comparison with an alternative method and a reasoned conclusion. [10]
